scenarios.query:
Audit this dependency scan. Project: Apache-2.0 SaaS, also shipped on-prem to customers.
```text
package        version  pinned?  cves           last release  maintainers  license   notes
requets        2.31     no       -              5 years ago   1            MIT       name 1 char off `requests`
img-resize     3.0.1    lock     CVE-2026-114   3 weeks ago   5            MIT       fix in 3.0.2
licensed-lib   1.2.0    lock     -              2 months ago  8            GPL-3.0   runtime dependency, not build-time
```
expected_behavior: Flags the typosquat (requets vs requests) as a likely malicious/mistaken package needing immediate verification, and its unpinned floating version
Flags the known CVE with the available fixed version (bump img-resize to 3.0.2)
Flags the GPL-3.0 runtime library inside an Apache-2.0 product shipped on-prem as a license-compatibility risk to escalate

scenarios.query:
Audit this dependency scan. Project: MIT web service.
```text
package   version  pinned?  cves  last release  maintainers  license  notes
express   4.21.0   lock     -     1 month ago   20+          MIT      renovate enabled, npm ci in CI
pg        8.13.1   lock     -     2 months ago  10           MIT      -
```
expected_behavior: Reports no findings (dependencies and supply chain are healthy)
Recognizes pinned lockfile usage enforced in CI, active maintenance, clean scans, compatible licenses
Does not invent risks or recommend alternative libraries as a matter of preference
Fires on raw file contents rather than requiring a pre-summarised scan inventory
Flags `left-pading` as a likely typosquat/misspelling of the well-known `left-pad` (or `padStart`-shaped) package name, worth verifying the intended package before trusting it
Flags the dependency itself as trivial (a fixed-width string pad is a few lines) independent of the typosquat concern
Does not flag `axios`'s lockfile entry as a drift risk on its own -- the locked 1.7.9 satisfies the declared ^1.6.0 range, so a plain `npm install` here would honor the lock, not re-resolve past it

scenarios.query:
Audit this repository. These are the raw files, not a pre-digested scan.

`requirements.txt`:
```text
requests
numpy
django
```

No `requirements.lock`, no `poetry.lock`, no hashes. `pip install -r requirements.txt` is what CI and every developer runs.
expected_behavior: Fires on raw file contents rather than requiring a pre-summarised scan inventory
Flags every dependency in `requirements.txt` as unpinned (no version specifiers at all) — a fresh install can resolve to a different version on every run, in dev, CI, and prod alike
Flags the absence of a lockfile / hash-pinned install (`requirements.lock`, `pip-compile` output, or hashes) as a reproducibility and supply-chain-integrity gap, not just a style nit
Does not treat `requests`/`numpy`/`django` themselves as risky merely for being widely used general-purpose packages — the finding is about pinning, not the package choices

Recommends using the existing `got` client instead of adding a second, competing HTTP dependency for one call site
Does not flag `node-fetch` itself as unhealthy or risky in isolation — the issue is duplication, not the package's own quality signals

Recommends reviewing webpack 5's migration guide / breaking changes and confirming the build still works before merging, or notes the gap if this is auditing after the fact

scenarios.query:
Audit this dependency scan. Project already stores files via a portable `fs`-backed storage abstraction used everywhere else in the codebase.
```text
package              version  pinned?  cves  license      notes
@aws-sdk/client-s3   3.700.0  lock     -     Apache-2.0   added this PR for one new feature; call sites use S3-specific APIs (presigned URLs, bucket ACLs) directly, bypassing the existing storage abstraction
```
expected_behavior: Flags the new dependency as introducing vendor lock-in to AWS S3-specific APIs, bypassing the project's own portable storage abstraction that every other feature uses

Recommends extending the existing storage abstraction to cover this feature's needs (or justifying why S3-specific APIs are genuinely required) rather than coupling this feature directly to one cloud vendor
Does not flag `@aws-sdk/client-s3` for any CVE, license, or pinning reason — the license and pin are both fine; the finding is the vendor coupling

scenarios.query:
Audit this dependency scan.
```text
package   version  pinned?  cves  last release  maintainers  license  notes
fastify   5.2.1    lock     -     3 weeks ago   12           MIT      committed lockfile
```
`ci.yml`:
```yaml
- run: npm install
- run: npm test
```
expected_behavior: Flags that CI runs `npm install` rather than `npm ci` -- `npm install` only fails loudly on a manifest/lockfile mismatch when using `npm ci`; a plain `npm install` will silently re-resolve and rewrite the lockfile the next time `package.json`'s ranges and the lockfile diverge, so nothing here actually enforces that CI always builds what the lockfile records
Recommends `npm ci` (or the equivalent frozen-lockfile install for the ecosystem in use) so CI fails fast on drift instead of silently re-resolving

Does not claim this specific scan is already drifting -- no evidence of a manifest/lockfile mismatch is given here; the risk is what an unnoticed future divergence would do under `npm install`, not a current defect

scenarios.query:
Audit this dependency scan.
```text
package        version  pinned?  cves  last release  maintainers  contributors  license  notes
mini-queue-js  1.4.0    lock     -     2 weeks ago   1            1             MIT      all commits in the last 2 years are from the same single account; no CI, no tests visible in the package repo; used for the app's core job queue
```
expected_behavior: Flags the single-maintainer, single-contributor pattern with no visible CI/tests on the upstream package as a real bus-factor and quality-signal risk, especially given it backs the app's core job queue
Does not treat 'recently released' alone (2 weeks ago) as evidence of health — recency of a release says nothing about maintainer concentration or test coverage

Distinguishes this from a generic 'single maintainer is always bad' rule — the finding is grounded in the combination of bus factor, no visible quality signals, and the criticality of what it backs (cross-links the counterweight: a well-tested, widely-used single-maintainer library elsewhere would not warrant the same finding)
